name: chmod
tasks: give a group read access to a folder

examples.does: Let the owner run the script
Owner read/write, group read, others nothing
Group can read everything and open folders (X: folders and already-executable files only)
Copy the permissions of another file

pitfalls: chmod -R 777 is almost never the fix: it lets every user change the files.
Numbers: 4 read, 2 write, 1 execute, for owner, group and others. 640 = rw- r-- ---.

name: chown
summary: Change the owner and group of files
tasks: give a folder to the web server user

examples.does: Set owner and group of one item
Set owner and group of a whole folder
Change a symbolic link itself, not its target

name: getfacl
tasks: why can this user read the file

examples.does: Owner, group and any extra user or group rules

pitfalls: A + at the end of the permissions in ls -l (drwxr-x---+) means an ACL is set.

name: setfacl
summary: Give one user or group extra permissions (ACL)
tasks: give one user access to a folder

examples.does: Let user alice read and enter a folder
Group devs can read and write everything already there
New files created here get the same rule (default ACL)
Remove all ACL rules from a file

pitfalls: -R changes what exists now. Add a default rule (-d) for files created later.

name: id
tasks: which groups is a user in

examples.does: Your user ID, group and all your groups
The same for another user
Group names only

pitfalls: A group added with usermod takes effect at the user's next login.

name: useradd

examples.does: Create a user with a home folder and bash
Same, and allow sudo (member of group sudo)
A system account for a service: no login shell

pitfalls: Without -m, no home folder is created.
Set a password afterwards with passwd, or the account cannot log in with one.
On Ubuntu, adduser asks for everything interactively and is easier by hand.

name: usermod
tasks: add a user to a group

examples.does: Add a user to a group, keeping their other groups
Lock the password (SSH keys still work)
Stop the user getting a shell

pitfalls: Without -a, -G replaces ALL the user's extra groups with the ones listed.

name: userdel

examples.does: Delete the account, keep the home folder
Delete the account, home folder and mail spool

pitfalls: Files the user owned elsewhere keep the old number as owner. Find them with: sudo find / -xdev -nouser

name: passwd

examples.does: Set a user's password
Password status: P set, L locked, NP none
Lock the password
Make the user choose a new password at next login

pitfalls: Locking the password does not stop SSH key logins. To block a user fully, also set an expired date: sudo chage -E 0 alice

name: chage
tasks: disable an account on a date

examples.does: Expiry dates for password and account
Password must change every 90 days
Account stops working after this date
Disable the account now (any login method)
Create a group
Create it with a chosen group ID (same ID on every server)

name: gpasswd
tasks: remove a user from a group

examples.does: Remove a user from one group
Add a user to one group

name: sudo
summary: Run a command as root or another user
tasks: what am I allowed to run with sudo

examples.does: What you may run with sudo
A root login shell (exit to leave)
Run a command as another user
Forget the cached password; the next sudo asks again

pitfalls: Edit sudo rules only with visudo. A syntax error in /etc/sudoers can lock everyone out of sudo.

name: visudo
tasks: give a user sudo rights for one command

examples.does: Edit one rules file; it is checked before saving
Check every sudo rules file for mistakes

pitfalls: Files in /etc/sudoers.d/ whose names contain a dot or end in ~ are ignored.

name: su

examples.does: Log in as alice (her environment, her home folder)
Get a shell as a service user that has no login shell

pitfalls: On Ubuntu root has no password by default, so su - fails; use sudo -i.

name: w
summary: Who is logged in and what they are running

examples.does: Logged-in users, where from, idle time and current command
Same, without the header

name: who
summary: Logged-in users and the last boot

examples.does: Logged-in users
Time of the last boot

name: last

examples.does: The last 20 logins
Reboot history
One user's logins, with the remote host shown last

pitfalls: Failed logins are not here: use sudo lastb, or journalctl -u ssh.
